text: Let’s start with three numbers: 8, 3, and 5.
Compare the first two elements, 8 and 3.
8 is greater than 3. Swap the first two.
Now compare the second and third elements.
8 is greater than 5. Swap those two elements.
Compare 3 and 5. They are already in order.
The array is sorted. Highlight all three elements.
Create an array with 4, 7, 2, and 9.
Highlight the first element. Its index is zero.
Insert 6 at the second position.
Delete the third element, which is now 7.
Highlight the largest number, 9.
Create a stack with 2 at the bottom and 4 on top.
Push 8 onto the stack.
Push 5. It becomes the new top.
Pop the stack. 5 leaves first.
The top is now 8. Highlight it.
Create a queue with 3, 5, and 8.
Enqueue 2. It joins at the rear.
Dequeue. 3 leaves from the front.
Dequeue again. This time 5 leaves.
8 is now at the front. Highlight it.
Create a linked list with 10, 20, and 30.
Visit the head node, 10.
Insert 15 after the first node.
Delete the second node. Connect 10 back to 20.
Visit the last node, 30. Its next pointer is null.
Let’s follow one instruction through the system. The teacher says, swap the first two numbers.
The microphone sends audio to the Python backend. Whisper turns the speech into recognized text.
The language model identifies the intent. It produces a structured swap event for positions zero and one.
Validation checks the schema, confidence, and current scene. Both positions exist, so this event can continue.
The accepted event crosses to the frontend scene manager. It applies the swap in order, preserving the rest of the scene.
The renderer selects a reusable SVG or Canvas template. The two elements move smoothly to their new positions.
The animated diagram reaches the classroom display. The teacher’s explanation and the visible change stay connected.
The teacher can pause, undo, or correct an operation. Undo restores the earlier scene through the scene manager.
Now follow the uncertain-event path. The teacher says, delete the fifth node, but only three nodes exist.
Whisper transcribes the sentence. Recognizing the words does not yet mean the instruction is safe to apply.
The intent parser proposes deleting index four. The proposed event still needs to be checked against the scene.
Validation finds that index four does not exist. The event is rejected before anything on the whiteboard changes.
Error handling withholds the uncertain event and sends it to the teacher for correction. The original scene stays intact.
The teacher corrects the instruction to delete the third node. The correction is checked again before it is accepted.
The scene manager applies the corrected, valid event. The list now contains ten and twenty.
The template renderer removes the third node and reconnects the remaining diagram.
The corrected diagram is displayed. A mistaken instruction was caught, corrected, and applied without corrupting the scene.
Let’s follow a drop of water. The sun warms the lake and provides energy for the water cycle.
Some liquid water changes into water vapor and moves into the air. This process is evaporation.
As moist air cools, water vapor condenses into tiny droplets. These droplets form a cloud.
When droplets grow large enough, water falls back to Earth as rain. This is precipitation.
Water flows downhill over the land, into streams, and back toward the lake. This movement is surface runoff.
Some water also soaks into the soil. It can replenish groundwater, which moves slowly beneath the surface.
Now let’s use an illustrative rainfall graph. On our first example day, ten millimeters of rain fell.
On day two, thirty millimeters fell. That is three times the rainfall on day one.
Day three brought twenty millimeters. These made-up values total sixty millimeters over three days, showing how a spoken explanation can build a graph.
